subject: tardigrade
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: tardigrade.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm brainstorming unexpected stylistic directions for a tardigrade model — considering Victorian scientific plates, stained glass, inflatable pool toys, art-nouveau jewelry — and leaning toward a Delft blue-and-white porcelain aesthetic.

Now I'm planning the figurine's palette: cobalt scrollwork and floral motifs against white glaze, with small gold-lustre accents on the claws and mouth ring for extra richness.

I'm also mapping out tardigrade anatomy for accuracy — the plump segmented body, four pairs of stubby clawed legs, a terminal mouth ring with lamellae, eyespots, and head cirri — while deciding to scale the figurine up to a more tangible, displayable size rather than its microscopic real-world dimensions.

Now I'm working out the skeletal proportions: a body roughly 0.5 m long positioned horizontally with legs splayed downward and outward, the rear pair angled backward, and figuring out body radius, height placement, and leg length so the claws rest naturally on the ground.

I'm building the spine chain from tail to head, adding a head joint with a jaw featuring a small snout, lips, and a stylet, then lofting the body with stations that taper from a narrow tail through a fat midsection to a narrower head.

For coloring, I'm thinking of a Delft-style paint: a white glaze base with cool blue-grey shading, plus cobalt segmentation bands and dorsal spot patterns along the body, with lighter belly tones and possibly subtle craquelure for the pooled cobalt look.

Writing paint shader logic...

I'll make the head a separate ellipsoid piece overlapping the body's tapered front end, attached at its own joint, rather than part of the body loft. For the rig, I'll set up a root joint at the hips with the spine chain running from tail to head, keeping a single root as required.

Building out the spine chain with four resampled joints, then attaching a head joint at the path's end parented to the last spine joint. Now I'm setting up the tail chain similarly, branching backward from the hips.

Then I move to the four leg pairs, computing their body-side attachment points along the z-axis and working out hip-to-foot limb geometry with appropriate segment lengths based on root-to-target distances.

For the feet, I'm adding 4 small curved claws per foot arranged in a ring around the ankle tip, matching the tardigrade's characteristic multi-claw stumpy legs.

Working through the tilt angle convention, I estimate the downward dip from a 55-degree lean would pull the claw tip about 0.037 below the foot, so I'll set foot height to 0.04 as a reasonable safety margin without being able to verify exact floor contact beforehand.

Rather than post-computing bounds and shifting the root afterward, which feels risky, I decide to build each claw with explicit base-to-tip spike geometry instead, computing tip positions directly in model space as foot position plus a small splay in x/z and a fixed downward offset, giving deterministic floor contact for all four claws by design.

I'll curve the claws using a bezier sweep tapering to a point, tinted gold for a lustrous accent against the Delft blue, and add similar gold touches to the mouth ring and eye rims. For the legs, I'll build flattened foot pads and paint subtle blue stripe bands along their length using a shared glaze function.

Now I'm shaping the head itself: an ellipsoid skull with a stylised tardigrade mouth made of upper and lower jaw domes, a dark inner cavity, and a tiny ring of cobalt stylet teeth, positioned near the front of the head.

Adding teeth rings...

Now thinking about tardigrade identity cues — segmented plump body, folded ridges, eight clawed legs, a snout, and cirri (sensory hairs) on the head sides, which I'll add as small paired spikes near the head.

For body segmentation, I'm planning ring-shaped fold ridges around the torso using loop geometry cut along the spine axis, then sweeping thin tubes to form relief bands at several points along the body, complementing the painted color bands rather than replacing them.

I'm computing rosette centers for each segment, then working out how to loop a sweep around the body at fixed z-heights for the raised ridge rings, keeping the loft and leg geometry separate so the ridges don't interfere. I'm deciding the ridge color should be flat blue, though gold might work too.

Now I'm thinking about adding a dorsal row of small raised tubercles along the spine, using a sweep or scatter function to place stick spheres along the body's top surface by sampling frame points along the loft path.

For flank detailing, I'm weighing scatter-placed pearl dots versus a cheaper paint-based pattern, leaning toward a paint function that computes color per-point based on position and normal to produce a scalloped wave pattern on the sides.

Writing paint shader logic...

Working out the rosette placement...

Now I'm working out the head paint, planning a white base with blue crown spots and light blue cheek blush using a countershade and spots combination from the SDK's paint functions, then moving on to leg painting.

For the legs I'm using blue stripes along the y-axis with a slight wobble for a countershaded band look, and considering corrugated telescoping geometry by making the leg radius oscillate with a cosine function along its sweep for a ridged appearance instead of separate ring geometry.

Now I'm setting up the leg chain with hip, knee, and ankle joints uniquely named per side (L/R mapped to +X/-X), so the limb function produces root, knee, and foot points to sweep the leg mesh along with the ridged radius function.

I'm computing the foot target position and verifying the distance from the hip root against the segment lengths to confirm the leg needs to bend outward and slightly upward at the knee, keeping the bend direction consistent with the body's bottom boundary.

For the hind legs, I'm placing the root near the hips and the foot target further back and inward, noting the tardigrade has no real tail so the rear end should just be rounded off rather than extending a tail chain. I'm setting up the spine rig so it extends back to a hip joint for the rear pair.

Now I'm working out the body's overall length along z, from rear to the head tip including the mouth, landing on roughly 0.64 meters, and spacing out the four leg positions evenly along that span with each segment about 0.055 apart.

Defining cross-section stations along the body...

Mapping out the spine and tail chains: spine joints resampled across four segments from hips to head, tail chain split into two joints tapering down and back. The loft bone connects tail, hips, and spine consistently with how the core joint pattern worked in the earlier example, sharing the hips point as the common origin.

For the head, I'm setting up a loft path running from tail through to the head, confirming bones can extend slightly past geometry endpoints without issue, and checking that the `bone: [tail, hips, spine]` array syntax works with the loft function as documented. Now I'm working out the eye decals — placing them on a head ellipsoid built from a sphere geometry scaled down and positioned at the head joint, with mirrored decals for symmetry.

Positioning the eye hit point using azimuth angles on the head surface, and thinking through the decal texture design: a Delft-style eye with a cobalt outer ring, white ring, and layered iris details rendered as SVG.

Now I'm working out the sensory cirri hairs on the head—using bezier sweeps from surface hit points to create thin tapered hairs with gilded sphere tips, placed in pairs at specific azimuth/elevation angles so they point outward and slightly backward like a real tardigrade's head bristles.

I'm also adding the mouth lamellae, peribuccal papillae, and reconsidering the dorsal pearl color (maybe pale blue instead of gold to fit the Delft palette), plus deciding whether to add gold lustre accents on the claws and mouth rim. I'm tempted to hide a tiny "DELFT" maker's mark decal on the underside like a porcelain signature, but it'd be invisible, so I'm weighing whether it's worth including.

Instead I'm placing a proper Delft medallion decal on both flanks—a cobalt windmill scene in a circular frame with white background and blue border—positioned to overlay cleanly against the rosette pattern already there. Since the decal faces outward in whatever direction it's placed, I don't think I need to mirror it for the opposite side; both flanks should read correctly without flipping the artwork.

I'm checking that the medallion's position doesn't collide with the leg attachment points, and it looks clear since the medallion sits above the leg zone. I'll skip extra details like a wavy dorsal border and keep the glaze material simple with moderate roughness. For the texture set I'm settling on a handful of distinct decals: an eye texture, the medallion, and maybe a cheek blush, aiming for a reasonable total count.

Now I'm considering adding a small Delft tulip motif as a crown ornament on the head rather than scattering tulips along the dorsal ridge, since that keeps the design clean while still nodding to the iconic cobalt tulip imagery.

I'll add a scroll-pattern decal near the shoulder, settling on 4-5 textures total to keep things manageable within line budget. Now I'm working out the body ridge placement, counting 8 loops along the Z-axis boundaries and adjusting rosette positions relative to the body's vertical center.

For pearl placement along the body, I realize putting them on top at every segment would collide with the rosettes already sitting at φ=0 on even rows, so I'll restrict pearls to odd rows instead to avoid overlap.

Now I'm working out row parity by computing z0 and the k index ranges across the body length, figuring out which rows fall within -1 to 7 so I can pick the odd ones for pearl placement, settling on a light blue flattened sphere for the pearl color.

For the rosette angle snapping, I'm computing a per-row offset (0° or 30° alternating by parity) and then rounding the azimuthal angle to the nearest 60° increment plus that offset, so each row's pearls alternate in rotational phase to avoid aligning in straight columns.

I realize the belly region at φ=180° naturally lands on a cell center too, so I should suppress rosettes there (since the belly should stay flat white) rather than special-casing it away. Using an arc radius around 0.105 mm, the 60° spacing works out to roughly 0.11 m of arc per cell with 0.055 z-spacing between rows, so a flower radius of about 0.022 fits reasonably within each cell even when stretched.

Checking neighbor spacing: adjacent flowers in the same row sit ~0.11 apart, staggered rows ~0.078 apart diagonally, so a petal radius near 0.021–0.026 stays clear of overlaps. Computing the cell index, angular offset, and local polar coordinates to place a five-petaled rosette shape at each cell center...

I'm defining the petal outline band, a pooled blue fill, a white center ring, and a tiny deep-blue dot at the core, plus small accent dots at the midpoints between neighboring flowers for decorative sprigs.

I'm also figuring out segment-edge shading for ambient occlusion near ridges, blending warm white at the top to a cooler shade lower down, then planning the leg paint with countershaded stripes, gilt claws, white foot pads, and a mouth cavity with deep blue interior, white lips, and gilt teeth. Now I'm starting to write the TypeScript code that imports the geometry and painting utilities to build this Delftware-style creature.

Still writing the color palette and paint functions...

Still writing SVG code...

Adding windmill structure next—a trapezoid body, roof, hub, and rotated sails with lattice detailing, plus sky hatching, a wavy ground line, clouds, and tiny birds for the scene.

I'm considering adding a spiral scroll decoration but checking placement against the head and medallion to avoid overlap — it seems too tight near the shoulder, so I'm thinking of shifting it to the rear flank instead.

Since the rosette pattern underneath might visually clash with the scroll, I'm considering giving it a white backing patch, like a small cartouche, so it stands out cleanly against the existing paintwork. I'd also mirror the scroll decal on the opposite side for symmetry.

Now I'm sketching the claw geometry function, fanning each foot's claws across a horizontal arc outward from the leg direction, computing each claw's heading angle as an offset from the leg's outward-facing direction.

Still shaping the paw geometry...

Now I'm setting up the leg joint chains with hip, knee, and foot names per side, giving each a floor contact point under the foot. Then I'm working out the limb call parameters, deciding how to pass the bend direction for the leg segments.

Now I'm defining the four leg attachment points along the body with their z-positions, target points, and root/foot x-offsets, then checking each root point against the body's elliptical cross-section at that z to confirm it sits just inside the surface.

For parenting the legs to the spine chain, I'm matching each hip's z-position to the nearest spine joint (spine1 through spine4, with hips/tail1 for the rearmost), using a nearestJoint lookup to assign bones.

For the leg geometry, I'm sweeping a tapered radius profile along each leg chain with a cosine ripple for texture, converging to a narrow foot tip, and applying the body surface loops separately from the legs.

Now I'm positioning the head: an ellipsoid nested against the body front, with the jaw as a child joint pivoting near the mouth, and I'm placing upper lip geometry as a small flattened sphere near the front of the skull.

Continuing, I'm working out the mouth parts in detail—lower lip sphere on the jaw, a dark cavity ellipsoid tucked inside, and a ring of teeth positioned along the mouth opening, split into upper and lower arcs around the head and jaw bones.

For the teeth, I'm using small forward-pointing spike shapes in gold, placed on a ring of radius 0.034 centered near the lip area, checking that their size and placement nest just inside the lip dome's curved surface so they stay embedded rather than poking through.

Actually, I think I'll simplify the mouth design overall — using lip domes with a darker cavity ellipsoid tucked slightly in front between them to suggest depth, rather than fussing over exact tooth placement.

Adding cirri placement...

Placing the crown tulip decal on top of the head, oriented with up toward +Z so it reads correctly from above, positioned near the top surface point with appropriate size. Also setting eye placement angles and sizes before moving on to head details.

For glaze paint I'll use countershaded blue-white spots with a slight shade darkening, and plain flat cream color for the lips/mouth area instead of spots. Then for ridges along the body, I'm sweeping small loops at regular Z intervals along the body surface to create raised ring details.

Writing ridge sweep code...

Placing scroll cartouche decals...

Adjusting the cartouche sizing to [0.05,0.05] so it fits the ridge gap more cleanly. The medallion near -0.03 is trickier since it's wider than the ridge spacing there, so ridges would poke through it; I'm considering raising the decal's lift slightly so it clears the ridge tops instead of reworking the ridge geometry.

I'm figuring out the ridge geometry: keeping arcs near the top and bottom of the ring while leaving gaps on the sides for the medallion and cartouches, then concatenating the sliced loop segments to form the open path, relying on default round caps to close the ends.

I'm checking which ridge positions fall within the cartouche and medallion z-ranges, adjusting the medallion span down to 0.085 so it only clips ridge k3 while k4 stays just clear, and planning to use arc-only segments for the ridges that overlap these decorative bands.

Tallying parts: body, 8 ridges, 4 pearls, legs with claws totaling 48, eyes, cirri with balls, mouth with teeth, and decals comes to roughly 110 parts, which falls short of my 180-340 target, so I'll need to add more detail.

I'm considering extra embellishments like gold studs, a bead collar, and leg cuffs made from thin torus rings looped at each leg's joint or ankle for a decorative gold bangle effect.

Placing cuffs slightly up from the ankle along the shin direction to avoid hitting the rounded cap, using small sweeps with gold coloring — giving 8 gold cuffs plus blue knee rings for 16 extra decorative parts total. I'm also thinking about small touches like eyebrows or papillae around the mouth, though extra textures probably aren't necessary beyond that.

Skipping a dorsal tulip-card feature and any glow effects as unneeded extras, and now moving to write the final code, setting up imports from the builder library and sketching out helper calls for ring frames and joint types.

Writing body loft and joint setup...

Still writing leg specs...

Checking the bend plane for the leg joints using non-colinear knee hints, then verifying front and middle leg distances fall within reasonable bounds. I'm now working out claw heading angles for each leg relative to the body axis.

Writing claw sweep geometry...

Now I'm positioning the foot pad and checking its placement against the claw base, then setting up cuff rings along the leg sweep using loop placement at computed points with direction vectors from knee to foot and hip to knee.

With the leg radii settled, I'm moving on to the body paint function, blending shade and white lighting based on normal direction, adding segment edge darkening, and layering in a cellular crack pattern for surface texture.

I'm layering the petal rings with white highlights and deep outline bands, adding center dots, then moving to the medallion SVG with rotated sail lines radiating from the center point.

Adding clouds, sea, and windmill shapes...

Still writing tulip SVG...

Now sketching a scroll cartouche with a circular border and spiral curl paths inside to suggest a decorative S-scroll shape.

Still writing cirrus helper...
